core_idea: The picture behind most senses of **run** is movement that keeps going: a person on foot, water, a machine, a bus service, a road across the land, or a business that continues.

senses.definition: move quickly on foot, faster than when you walk, so that for a moment both feet are off the ground

examples.text: The dog ran across the yard to meet us.
I had to run to catch the bus.
Kim can run faster than anyone else in the class.
Don't run on the wet floor, or you'll fall.

synonyms.note: run as fast as you can for a short distance
run slowly and steadily for exercise
run a short way in a hurry

compare.note: when you walk, one foot is always on the ground

subsenses.definition: move fast on foot as a sport, either in a race or as regular exercise

examples.text: Mari runs every morning before work.
Ana ran her first marathon last spring.
The two brothers ran against each other in the final.

adaptation.grammar: The direction goes in a phrase after the verb: *run to the door*, *run across the street*, *run upstairs*. The verb itself says only how the person moves, so a language whose verbs of motion include the direction (one verb for *go in running*) needs to split the idea in two.

senses.definition: go somewhere quickly, or leave a place quickly in order to get away from someone or something

examples.text: Could you run to the store and get some bread?
I'd love to stay and talk, but I have to run.
When the alarm went off, everyone ran for the exits.
You can't run from your problems forever.

compare.note: the usual phrasal verb for leaving in order to escape

subsenses.definition: drive past a red light or a stop sign without stopping

examples.text: He got a ticket for running a red light.
Never run a stop sign, even when the road looks empty.

adaptation.semantic: In everyday American speech, *run to the store* or *run over to a friend's house* means make a quick trip, often by car; the person need not be on foot at all. Many languages keep the on-foot word separate from the quick-trip word.

senses.definition: be in charge of a business, a group, or an activity, and make the decisions about how it works

examples.text: Her parents run a small restaurant near the station.
Who runs this place?
The club is run by a group of volunteers.
Omar has been running the sales team for two years.

synonyms.note: more formal; for businesses, systems, and machines

compare.note: you can run a business that you do not own

adaptation.semantic: This everyday sense often needs a more formal verb in other languages, such as **manage**, **direct**, or **lead**. It covers businesses, schools, events, courses, websites, and households alike. Note the common passive with **by**: *the hotel is run by a family*.

senses.definition: be working or switched on, or make a machine, an engine, or a computer program work

examples.text: Is the engine still running?
Leave the computer running so the update can finish.
The heater runs on gas.
Run the program again and see if the error goes away.

synonyms.note: formal; for the use without an object
for the use without an object

subsenses.definition: do a test, a check, or a search, especially using a machine or a computer

examples.text: The doctor wants to run a few more tests.
I ran a search for the file but couldn't find it.
Let's run the numbers before we decide.

subsenses.definition: use a vehicle or a machine, paying for the fuel or the power it needs

examples.text: The old freezer costs a lot to run.
They can't afford to run two cars.

adaptation.grammar: Both the machine and the person can be the subject: *the engine runs*; *she runs the engine*. Some languages need two different verbs, one meaning work and one meaning make something work. A program also runs on a computer or a system, with **on**.

senses.definition: (of a bus, a train, or a plane) go along its route at regular times, or provide such a service

examples.text: Trains run every ten minutes during the day.
The last bus runs at midnight.
They're running extra buses because of the festival.
Does this line run on Sundays?

senses.definition: flow somewhere in a stream, or make water flow from a tap

examples.text: Tears ran down her cheeks.
Someone left the water running in the bathroom.
My nose has been running all day.
I'll run you a hot bath.

items: run the water until it gets hot

compare.note: water leaks when it escapes from where it should be
**pour** is faster and heavier, and is also what a person does with a liquid

subsenses.definition: (of color in cloth, paint, or makeup) spread when it gets wet

examples.text: Wash the red shirt separately, or the color will run.
The rain made the ink run.

adaptation.semantic: Many languages use the flow word only for water and a different word for a nose or eyes that produce liquid; English uses **run** for both. A color that runs is a separate word again in many languages, closer to **bleed** or **fade**.

senses.definition: continue for a particular length of time, or until a particular time

examples.text: The show ran for six months and then closed.
My contract runs until the end of the year.
The class runs from nine to eleven on Tuesdays.
The meeting ran an hour longer than planned.

items: run until the end of the month

adaptation.grammar: Use **for** with a length of time and **until** or **to** with an end point: *it runs for two hours*, *it runs until five*, *it runs from nine to five*. Not **during**: a class does not *run during two hours*.

senses.definition: go or stretch from one place to another in a particular direction

examples.text: The road runs along the river for several miles.
A fence runs around the whole field.
The border runs through the middle of the lake.
The wires run under the floor and up the wall to the socket.

subsenses.definition: put a wire, a pipe, or a cable so that it goes along a particular path

examples.text: We ran a cable from the house to the garage.
The electrician ran the new wires behind the wall.

subsenses.definition: (of a quality, a feeling, or an idea) be found all through a family, a group, or a piece of writing

examples.text: Musical talent runs in Yuki's family.
A feeling of hope runs through all her songs.
Curly hair runs in the family.

adaptation.semantic: For roads, borders, and lines, many languages say **go**, **pass**, or **stretch**. For a quality in a family they say *be inherited* or *be in the blood*; for an idea in a book, *pass through* or *fill*.

senses.definition: move your hand, a finger, or a tool quickly and lightly along or over something

examples.text: She ran her fingers through her hair.
He ran his hand along the smooth wood.
Ravi ran his eyes down the list of names.
Run a comb through your hair before we leave.

items: run a comb through your hair

adaptation.semantic: Many languages say **pass**, **slide**, or **move** here: *pass your hand over the wood*, *slide your fingers through your hair*. The English verb adds the idea of a quick, light, unbroken movement.

senses.definition: be or become in a particular state, for example low, dry, short, or late

examples.text: We're running low on milk.
The well ran dry during the summer.
Sorry, I'm running a little late.
We're running short of time, so let's move on.

synonyms.note: the general verb; **run** is used only with a small set of adjectives

adaptation.grammar: Only a small set of adjectives follows **run** in this sense: **low**, **short**, **dry**, **late**, **cold**, **wild**, **high**, **deep**, and a few more. It is not a general word for become; use **get** or **become** with other adjectives.

senses.definition: try to be elected to a political position

examples.text: She's running for mayor next year.
He ran against a much more experienced candidate and lost.
Are you going to run again?
Sam decided to run for a seat on the city council.

synonyms.note: the usual British verb: *stand for election*

compare.note: **campaign** is what a candidate does after deciding to run

adaptation.culture: American English usually says *run for office*; British English has traditionally preferred *stand for election*, though **run** is now common in both. The position follows **for**: *run for mayor*, *run for the council*.

senses.definition: be at a particular level or amount, or cost a particular amount of money

examples.text: Prices are running about ten percent higher than last year.
The repair bill ran to more than a thousand dollars.
He's running a fever, so he should stay in bed.
Interest rates are running at their highest level in years.

synonyms.note: for a level: *unemployment stands at five percent*

senses.definition: print or show a news story or an advertisement in a newspaper or on television, or be printed or shown in this way

examples.text: The paper ran the story on its front page.
They're running the ad on television all week.
The interview runs in tomorrow's edition.

adaptation.semantic: Other languages normally say **publish**, **print**, or **broadcast**; **run** is the everyday word of newspapers and television in English, and works both with an object (*run a story*) and without one (*the story ran*).

senses.definition: take someone or something somewhere quickly, especially in a car

examples.text: I can run you to the station if you like.
Can you run these papers over to the office?
Lee ran me home after practice.

synonyms.note: the neutral verb; **run** suggests a short, quick trip

subsenses.definition: take goods such as guns or drugs into a country illegally

examples.text: He was arrested for running guns across the border.
The gang had been running drugs into the city for years.

adaptation.semantic: This informal sense usually means give someone a ride in a car on a short trip, or take something somewhere quickly. Languages without a light verb for this say **drive** or *take by car*.

phrases.definition: escape from someone or from danger by going as fast as you can

examples.text: The door was open, so we ran for it.
When the guard turned around, the boys ran for it.

phrases.definition: working as it should, especially after being set up or fixed

examples.text: The new website should be up and running by Monday.
It took a week to get the system up and running again.

phrases.definition: act or grow freely, without anyone keeping control
phrases.explanation: Used of children and animals, of plants in a garden, and of the imagination.

examples.text: The kids ran wild in the yard all afternoon.
Since nobody has lived there, the garden has run wild.
Let your imagination run wild and draw whatever you like.

phrases.definition: (of feelings) be very strong, so that people may become angry or upset

examples.text: Feelings were running high on both sides of the argument.
Tempers ran high at the meeting.

phrases.definition: (of a feeling or a difference between people) be very strong and have existed for a long time

examples.text: Her love of the sea runs deep.
The differences between the two families run deep.

phrases.definition: take an idea or a plan and develop it with energy

examples.text: Kim liked the idea and decided to run with it.
Give the team a clear goal and let them run with it.

phrases.definition: still going, but with almost no energy, money, or strength left

examples.text: By the end of the week, the whole team was running on empty.
The charity has been running on empty for months.

adaptation.culture: The picture is a car whose fuel gauge shows empty but is still moving.

synonym_discrimination.note: **Run** is the general word for moving fast on foot: *She ran to catch the bus*. **Jog** means run slowly and steadily, usually for exercise: *He jogs around the park every morning*. **Sprint** means run as fast as you can for a short distance, often in a race: *The players sprinted for the ball*.

usage_note: For elections, American English usually says *run for office*; British English has traditionally preferred *stand for election*, though **run** is now common in both. In American English, *run to the store* or *run over to someone's house* is a quick trip by any means, not necessarily on foot.

learner_errors.incorrect: I have ran three miles today.
learner_errors.correct: I have run three miles today.
learner_errors.note: The past tense is **ran**, but the past participle used after **have** and in the passive is **run**.

learner_errors.incorrect: The film runs during two hours.
learner_errors.correct: The film runs for two hours.
learner_errors.note: A length of time takes **for**; **during** goes with a named period such as *the summer* or *the meeting*.

adaptation.semantic: Other languages often have one word for a person running and use other verbs for the rest: a business is managed, a machine works, water flows, a bus goes, a road goes, a story appears. Translate each sense by its meaning, not by the word **run**.
adaptation.grammar: **Run** is irregular: *run, ran, run*. The past participle after **have** and in the passive is **run**, not **ran**. Many senses are used both with and without an object: *the engine runs*, *she runs the engine*; *the story ran*, *the paper ran the story*.
adaptation.pronunciation: The vowel is the short **u** of **cup** and **sun**, so the word rhymes with **fun**. The past tense **ran** has the vowel of **cat**. The spelling doubles the **n** in **running** and **runner**.
